name: Records of the Grand Historian
info: The Records of the Grand Historian, or Shiji, is a Chinese history written in the late 2nd and early 1st centuries BCE by Sima Qian, building on his father's work, and the first of the Twenty-Four Histories of imperial China.

facts.made: Sima Qian, Grand Historian at the Han court and generally credited as the author, who continued the work begun by his father Sima Tan
facts.form: A history in literary Chinese of about 526,500 characters in 130 chapters, in five sections: Basic Annals, Tables, Treatises, Hereditary Houses and Ranked Biographies; first written on bamboo slips
facts.where: Only two fragments of pre-Tang manuscripts survive, both at the Ishiyama-dera temple in Ōtsu, Japan; portions of nine Tang manuscripts are at Dunhuang and in Japanese temples and museums; read today in printed editions
facts.known: The model for later dynastic histories; the Ranked Biographies; a span from the Yellow Emperor to Emperor Wu of Han; use of eyewitness accounts; a rich source of chengyu idioms; the biographies of Confucius and Qin Shi Huang

t: Sima Qian continued a history planned by his father Sima Tan and carried it from the legendary Yellow Emperor to the reign of Emperor Wu of Han, in about 526,500 characters.
Instead of one continuous narrative, he broke history into annals, tables, treatises, hereditary houses and biographies, a plan that set the model for all later dynastic histories of China.
The text was hidden for about twenty years after Sima Qian's death, lost ten chapters and gained additions from other hands, and its earliest surviving manuscript pieces are held in Japan.
dyk: The Shiji was written on bamboo slips of 24 to 36 characters each. Endymion Wilkinson calculates that the whole work would have made between 466 and 700 bundles weighing 40 to 60 kilograms.
ev: Sima Tan, Grand Historian at the Han court, drafts plans for the work and leaves fragments and notes
Sima Tan dies and his son Sima Qian continues and completes the work
The manuscript is more or less complete and is hidden in the residence of Sima Qian's daughter Sima Ying
Ban Biao and Ban Gu claim that ten chapters of the Shiji are lacking
Pei Yin writes one of the commentaries most historical editions include
Sima Zhen and Zhang Shoujie write the other two commentaries later gathered as the Three Experts' annotations
The earliest surviving woodblock printed editions are produced in the Song dynasty (960–1279)
The Zhonghua Book Company publishes its ten-volume edition, revised in 1982

sections.origins:
The Shiji began as the project of Sima Tan, who was Grand Historian (Taishi, also translated Grand Scribe) of the Han dynasty court during the late 2nd century BCE. He drafted plans for an ambitious work and left behind fragments and notes that may have been incorporated into the final text. His son Sima Qian succeeded him in the post after Sima Tan's death in 110 BCE and is generally credited as the author. The family were hereditary historians to the Han emperor, so Sima Qian had access to the early Han archives, edicts and records.

The history he undertook covers a period of about 2,500 years, from the age of the legendary Yellow Emperor to the reign of Emperor Wu of Han in the author's own time, and it describes the world as it was known to the Chinese of the Western Han dynasty. Sima Qian also had ancient books, written on bamboo and wooden slips, from before the Han, and many of the sources he used have not survived. Besides archives and imperial records, he interviewed people and travelled around China to verify information. For the genealogies from the Yellow Emperor to the Gonghe regency (841 to 828 BCE) he used The Annals of the Five Emperors and the Classic of History.
sections.content:
The Shiji runs to around 526,500 Chinese characters, four times the length of Thucydides' History of the Peloponnesian War and longer than the Hebrew Bible. Sima Qian arranged its 130 chapters in five sections. The Basic Annals (twelve chapters) resemble the court chronicles of earlier tradition: the first five cover periods such as the Five Emperors or dynasties such as the Xia, Shang and Zhou, and the last seven cover individual rulers from the First Emperor of Qin to the first emperors of the Han. Sima chose to include de facto rulers such as Xiang Yu and Empress Dowager Lü and to leave out rulers who held no real power.

The Tables (chapters 13 to 22) set out reigns, events and royal lineages in tabular form, because, in Sima Qian's words, "the chronologies are difficult to follow when different genealogical lines exist at the same time." The Treatises (chapters 23 to 30) are the shortest section and treat ritual, music, pitch pipes, the calendar, astronomy, sacrifices, rivers and waterways, and financial administration. The Hereditary Houses (chapters 31 to 60) give chronicle-like accounts of leading Zhou states such as Qin and Lu in the earlier chapters and biographies in the later chapters on the Han. The Ranked Biographies (chapters 61 to 130) make up 42% of the whole.
sections.making:
Sima Qian conceived and composed the work in self-contained units, with a good deal of repetition between them. The date of completion is unknown, but it is certain that he finished it before 86 BCE, about the year he died. One copy was to reside in the imperial capital Chang'an, present-day Xi'an, and the other was probably stored in his home. In the Letter to Ren An, composed in the Zhenghe era of Emperor Wu's reign, he describes the work as spanning the time from the Yellow Emperor to the present and consisting of ten tables, twelve basic annals, eight treatises, thirty chapters on hereditary houses and seventy biographies, a total of 130 chapters.

He often names his sources, writing for example in the first chapter, "I have read the Spring and Autumn Annals and the Guoyu." He wrote of the problems of incomplete and contradictory sources: he noted that Qin Shi Huang burned the chronicle records of the Zhou states kept in the royal archive, and that the chronologies and genealogies of different ancient texts "disagree and contradict each other throughout." Of one table he wrote, "I have set down only what is certain, and in doubtful cases left a blank." His manuscript was written on bamboo slips and assembled into bundles of around 30 slips.
sections.reception:
Little is known about the early reception and circulation of the Shiji. After about 91 BCE the more or less completed manuscript was hidden in the residence of the author's daughter, Sima Ying, to avoid destruction under Emperor Wu and his immediate successor Emperor Zhao. It was finally disseminated during the reign of Emperor Xuan by Sima Qian's grandson through his daughter, Yang Yun, after a hiatus of around twenty years. The first commentaries date from the Northern and Southern dynasties (420 to 589) and the early Tang dynasty, and most historical editions include those of Pei Yin (5th century), Sima Zhen and Zhang Shoujie (both early 8th century).

Later readers praised its prose. Unlike subsequent official histories that adopted Confucian doctrine, proclaimed the divine rights of emperors and degraded any failed claimant to the throne, Sima Qian's more liberal and objective prose has been renowned and followed by poets and novelists. Scholars have questioned the historicity of his legendary kings. The Five Emperors are believed by modern scholars such as the Doubting Antiquity School to have been originally local deities, and Sima Qian was criticised for turning myths and folklore into sober history. Joseph Needham, writing in 1954, noted that twenty-three of the thirty Shang rulers' names appear on the Anyang bones, and concluded that Sima Qian had fairly reliable materials.
sections.survival:
The text circulated for many centuries as bundles of bamboo slips or small groups, and later on silk, which was lighter but expensive and rare. Until the work was transferred to paper, circulation was difficult and piecemeal, which accounts for many of the errors and variations in the text. Ten of the original 130 chapters were lost in the Eastern Han period (AD 25 to 220) and seem to have been reconstructed later. Several scholars of the 1st century BCE, such as Chu Shaosun, added interpolations, and Liu Zhiji reported the names of fifteen scholars supposed to have added material. Only Chu's additions are marked, with the words "Mr Chu said."

A large number of chapters on the first century of the Han correspond exactly to chapters of the Book of Han (Hanshu), and it is unclear which work they came from first. Yves Hervouet and A. F. P. Hulsewé argued that the originals of those chapters were lost and later reconstructed from the Hanshu. The earliest extant handwritten copy dates from 420 to 589. Only two fragments of pre-Tang manuscripts survive, both at the Ishiyama-dera temple in Ōtsu, Japan, with portions of nine Tang manuscripts: three from Dunhuang and six in Japanese temples and museums such as Kōzan-ji in Kyoto and the Tōyō Bunko in Tokyo.
sections.legacy:
The Shiji has been called a "foundational text in Chinese civilization." It set the model for all subsequent dynastic histories of China and is the first of the Twenty-Four Histories. Unlike Western historiographical conventions, it does not treat history as a continuous, sweeping narrative but breaks it into smaller, overlapping units on famous leaders, individuals and major topics. By providing definitive biographies of Confucius and Qin Shi Huang, Sima Qian is said to have shaped the enduring images of these two earlier figures and to have been one of the creators of Imperial China.

Its vivid accounts have made it a widely admired and frequently anthologised body of prose. With the Zuozhuan it is a rich source of chengyu, the four-character idiomatic phrases still used in modern Chinese, and the Ranked Biographies have supplied a large number of them. Its language, though literary Chinese, is relatively accessible to students with modest training, since it still shows influence from the author's spoken language. The primary modern edition is the Zhonghua Book Company's ten-volume edition of 1959, revised in 1982 and based on an edition made by Gu Jiegang in the early 1930s, and the Shiji has also been published there in simplified Chinese.

summary: The Records of the Grand Historian, or Shiji, is a Chinese history begun by Sima Tan and completed by his son Sima Qian, covering about 2,500 years from the Yellow Emperor to Emperor Wu of Han. It is the first of the Twenty-Four Histories and the model for those that followed.
references: Grant Hardy, Worlds of Bronze and Bamboo: Sima Qian's Conquest of History (Columbia University Press, 1999)
Burton Watson, Ssu Ma Ch'ien Grand Historian Of China (Columbia University Press, 1958)
Endymion Wilkinson, Chinese History: A New Manual (Harvard University Asia Center, 2012)
